title: Two providers, one consumer contract
summary: Follow real TMDB requests and the simulated ClientB backend into the same public SDK services, without confusing reference behavior with production guarantees.
body:
Substitutability has a precise scope

The target architecture is backend-agnostic: an application receives StreamCoreClient and shared StreamCore values, while each provider owns backend protocols and representations. This does not mean the backends offer identical products. TMDB supplies real authentication and catalogue requests, local reference subprofiles, and optional sample playback. ClientB supplies a simulated catalogue and account flow to exercise the same consumer contract. It is evidence that the boundary works, not evidence that a second production backend is integrated.

Trace TMDB from credentials to content

  1. The Android or browser factory creates platform storage and an HTTP client, then calls the internal shared factory. The HTTP client owns the base URL, optional bearer header, JSON handling, timeouts, and unsuccessful-response handling. Endpoint paths and query parameters belong in KtorTmdbApi.
  2. TmdbAuthenticateRepository.login requests a token, validates the supplied credentials, revokes a retained session when needed, creates a new session, loads the verified account, and persists it. Compensation handles an uncommitted remote session. AuthProvider.restoreSession() validates a stored session before restoring account identity; a configured expected account is a restriction, not an invented identity.
  3. Once an account exists, ProviderSessionFactory assembles its profile, home, details, search, playback, and content-policy adapters. TMDB profile records are local, account-scoped reference data. They are not TMDB household profiles returned by a remote profile API.
  4. Catalogue DTOs stay internal. The catalogue mapper translates numeric IDs, image paths, scores, dates, genres, and detail information into StreamCoreContent. The UI receives that shared representation. A provider's maturity rank is not a universal cross-provider policy.

Failure translation also belongs here. TmdbErrorMapper converts transport timeouts, IO, parsing, and HTTP failures into shared errors. A 401 or 403 during login means authentication failure; outside login it maps to unauthorized. HTTP 429 maps to a server error in the current implementation. Diagnostic source fields can retain provider context without making features import Ktor exceptions. Cancellation remains cancellation through the call executor.

Read configuration as ownership

StreamCoreConfiguration identifies the backend/environment, storage namespace, locale, optional region, persistence mode, and an optional expected-account restriction. TMDB's separate connection configuration contains its base URL and read token; its string representation redacts the token. Locale overrides endpoint language arguments; region is used on endpoints that accept it. ClientB's static reference catalogue does not become localized merely because the common configuration carries a locale.

ClientB login persists an account ID derived from the normalized identifier; its provider does not validate a real backend password. Its catalogue uses its own DTO vocabulary, then maps to shared content. Its account profile repositories live in memory for the client lifetime, including reference PIN scenarios; persistent auth or library storage does not make those simulated profile mutations durable.

Both providers default playback to Unsupported. Explicit demoPlayback = true advertises DemoMedia: TMDB resolves the Sintel sample; ClientB resolves a trick-play demonstration. These sources are not the selected catalogue film. QR login and password recovery remain unsupported; ClientB advertises reference PIN verification. Read capabilities and handle operation failures.

Exercise: locate the boundary for a new TMDB field

Suppose an endpoint gains an original-language field. Find the DTO, mapper, and shared model before touching a screen. Decide whether the field has a provider-neutral meaning. If so, define its absence semantics and map both providers; if not, keep it internal. Moving the entire DTO into a feature would make backend replacement a feature rewrite.

quiz.question: ClientB passes the same reference journey as TMDB. What does that establish?
options: Both providers have equivalent production authentication and catalogue services.
The simulated provider can satisfy the shared consumer contract for the exercised journey.
Every advertised feature can be enabled without runtime failure handling.
quiz.explanation: ClientB deliberately simulates backend behavior. Shared journeys demonstrate structural substitution and selected behavior, not production backend coverage.

title: Wire an application without owning SDK internals
summary: Choose a supported factory, give its client one owner, and keep UI state, navigation, resource presentation, and playback rendering in the application.
body:
Start at a factory, end at services

The current published targets are Android and Kotlin/Wasm wasmJs. Android supports the mobile, tablet, and TV application surfaces. Browser construction uses the Wasm factory. The existence of common Kotlin source is not an iOS, desktop JVM, Swift, or TypeScript SDK promise. A Node-based Wasm test exercises the in-memory consumer path; it does not make browser storage or createWeb a general Node integration.

ProviderEntrypointRequired inputs
TMDB AndroidTmdbSdk.createAndroidAndroid context and TmdbSdkConfiguration
TMDB browserTmdbSdk.createWebConfiguration; optional useSessionStorage
ClientB Android/browserClientBSdk.createAndroid / createWebMatching platform inputs and ClientBSdkConfiguration
ClientB in memoryClientBSdk.createInMemoryConfiguration; this factory forces in-memory persistence

The platform functions are extension functions in the provider package, so import createAndroid or createWeb as well as the factory object. Every entrypoint returns StreamCoreClient. There is no public TMDB createInMemory factory: select in-memory persistence through its platform configuration when appropriate.

Use the application's actual composition pattern

The Android flavor's ProviderModules.kt registers one client as a Koin singleton and closes it with onClose. SdkServicesModule.kt registers that same client's auth, profiles, home, details, search, library, and playback services. It does not construct a client per screen or register provider repositories. The TMDB app deliberately enables demo playback and uses the provider's current namespaced storage defaults. A new consumer should enable demo playback only when sample media is intended.

WebGraph.kt follows the same ownership pattern using TmdbSdk.createWeb. It calls sdk.auth.restoreSession(), detects a storage failure, and closes a failed graph before the host chooses its storage fallback. Android storage uses app-owned files; the browser factory selects local or session storage. Namespace ownership prevents two live instances from owning the same underlying stores in the current process/module. Closing the client releases its owned work and resources.

Features consume constructor-injected services. HomeViewModel calls HomeService, maps collections to application RowModel values, and combines them with progress for display. This is presentation work. The SDK owns account/profile authorization and saved-progress rules. TvHomeRoute obtains the ViewModel at the route boundary, collects state with lifecycle awareness, and connects navigation; the screen renders. Keep editor drafts, focus, responsive placement, and navigation out of providers.

Optional UI is resource presentation

sdk-ui exposes error-presentation contracts, common strings, and avatar artwork resolution. Provider UI artifacts supply provider wording, avatar-ID mappings, and artwork. They are optional Compose resource adapters, not screens, ViewModels, navigation, or DI containers. The app registers a provider mapper and resolver; a headless consumer omits them. A null avatar resource can be handled by the application's existing fallback rendering.

Playback has another deliberate seam. PlaybackService resolves media and owns progress operations. PlayerViewModel creates one application playback session from PlaybackSessionFactory, prepares it, reports progress events, and closes it in onCleared. Android Media3 and browser playback modules provide engines and surfaces. Register the factory, not one shared player session. Neither engine belongs in a published headless SDK dependency graph.

Exercise: integrate a headless consumer

Follow the independent SdkConsumerJourney: call auth.restoreSession(), login, call beginEntry, handle ready/choice/PIN/no-profile outcomes, then request content for the activated profile. Keep a single client owner and close it in a finally block. Identify which lines would change to replace ClientB with TMDB: construction and configuration change; the shared journey remains.

quiz.question: Where should a Media3 player session be created and closed?
options: Inside the provider's published playback repository.
As a singleton shared by every feature screen.
By its owning PlayerViewModel through an application playback-session factory.
quiz.explanation: The SDK resolves media and enforces progress rules. The application owns engine rendering and each ViewModel's playback-session lifetime.

title: Prove the boundary consumers actually use
summary: Distinguish source correctness, runtime contracts, dependency boundaries, published metadata, and independent consumer execution.
body:
Eight artifact families, three different audiences

The publishing convention explicitly assigns Maven names; Gradle project names alone do not define the public coordinates. The current local candidate uses group com.pampoukidis.streamcore and version 0.1.0-alpha02. There are eight artifact families, each with applicable KMP metadata and platform publications. A family is not a single physical file. The convention stages candidates locally and does not configure a release registry.

ArtifactPurpose
sdk-modelShared values, results, errors, requests, capabilities, context
sdk-apiConsumer client and service contracts
sdk-runtimeShared execution rules and provider integration infrastructure
provider-tmdbTMDB factory and internal backend adapters
provider-clientbSimulated ClientB factory and adapters
sdk-uiOptional shared presentation contracts and resources
provider-tmdb-uiOptional TMDB presentation adapters and artwork
provider-clientb-uiOptional ClientB presentation adapters and artwork

Distinguish three meanings of accessible code. Consumer API is what application features should call: StreamCoreClient, services, and models. Public provider SPI exists so another module can assemble a provider: the domain *Provider ports, ProviderSessionFactory, ProviderSessionServices, and ProviderOperationException. Runtime composition and storage infrastructure also cross provider-module boundaries. Their Kotlin visibility is not an invitation for features to bypass services. Internal runtime services, session mechanics, repositories, DTOs, and mappers remain implementation details.

Why dependency scopes matter

The provider builds export sdk-api with api, while runtime is an implementation dependency. The API exports models and coroutines because their types appear in public signatures. This lets a consumer declare a provider coordinate and compile against its returned client, without manually reproducing the SDK's dependency tree. implementation does not mean the runtime vanishes: implementation dependencies still participate in the resolved runtime closure. It controls exposure on consumer compile paths.

The five headless families reject UI, Koin, and playback-engine dependencies. The three optional UI families allow their resource closure while rejecting application features, runtime/provider data code, Koin, network/storage ownership, Material, Coil, and engines. Compose resource transitive dependencies make a simplistic “no Compose UI anywhere” check inappropriate for optional UI. The existing source, resolved-dependency, and metadata gates intentionally check different things.

Run the smallest evidence that answers the change

  1. Start with python tools/sdk/verify_sdk.py for source boundaries. It detects forbidden imports and unintended public implementation declarations. It is not a compiler, a binary compatibility checker, or proof of behavior.
  2. Run focused module host tests with :sdk:runtime:testAndroidHostTest or the changed provider's equivalent. The shared ProviderContract is compiled from sdk/testing/src/commonTest/kotlin into each provider's test source set. The registered :sdk:testing support project applies only Gradle's base plugin; it does not compile, run or publish these sources itself. Run the provider test tasks to execute the checks. The journey exercises validation, login, profile activation, catalogue operations, saved state, progress thresholds, unsupported playback without opt-in, logout/relogin, and repeated close. TMDB wraps controlled HTTP fixtures; ClientB uses its public in-memory factory.
  3. For storage changes, use restart and failure tests, not only in-memory happy paths. Android host restart coverage and browser storage restart coverage exercise platform behavior that common tests cannot establish.
  4. For publication or dependency changes, run tools/sdk/verify-publication.ps1. It stages artifacts, runs dependency and metadata gates, then builds/tests independent consumers. Optional Android resource device execution needs -AndroidSerial; without it the script builds that test APK but explicitly reports execution was not run.

The independent build in samples/sdk-consumer resolves Maven coordinates from staging and forbids composite substitution. Its Android consumer intentionally declares only provider dependencies; its headless Wasm journey executes ClientB, while TMDB is also a declared coordinate. Separate Android and browser consumers verify optional resources. Passing these checks establishes the tested publication boundary, not live TMDB credentials, production entitlement, or every app interaction.

Exercise: diagnose a checkout-only success

A feature compiles in the main repository but a coordinate consumer cannot see a shared return type. Inspect the owning public signature, api/implementation scopes, and staged metadata. Fix the publication relationship; adding a direct dependency to the sample can hide the broken consumer contract. Re-run the affected independent consumer after staging the fix.

quiz.question: Which check best catches a missing transitive compile dependency in a published provider?
options: A main-repository feature compile using project dependencies.
An independent consumer that declares only the staged provider coordinates.
A source search confirming that the dependency exists somewhere in the repository.
quiz.explanation: The separate consumer exercises actual publication metadata without checkout project or composite-build substitution.

title: Change the SDK without weakening its contract
summary: Place new data, operations, providers, policies, and storage changes at the boundary that owns them, then verify the affected consumer path.
body:
Begin with observable behavior

Before choosing files, state the consumer behavior: what input arrives, which account/profile owns it, which result or failure returns, and what survives restart. Separate a current invariant from a design proposal. The code already assigns authorization and shared saved-state rules to runtime, backend protocols to providers, and rendering to applications. A proposed download manager, entitlement policy, or new persistence engine is a future design decision, not an existing SDK guarantee. Favor one readable production path over interfaces created only to isolate a test.

Add a field with a meaning both providers can honor

For a content field, begin with StreamCoreContent.kt and decide units, absence semantics, and compatibility. Its release date already specifies epoch milliseconds with zero for unusable data; its maturity level explicitly remains provider-specific. Follow that precision. A default for a new serialized field can help old payloads decode, but does not automatically prove Kotlin binary compatibility. Review constructor and consumer changes as well as stored snapshots.

Update the provider DTO and mapper at the point where the value becomes known. TMDB summary and detail mapping may have different information; ClientB needs a deliberate reference value or absence. Search saved library/progress snapshots and sample data for the model's persistence and rendering uses. Extend the existing mapper and serialization tests for the meaning that changed, then compile the affected consumer surface. Do not add provider response types to shared models just to avoid mapping.

Add an operation at its real owner

  1. Define shared input/result types in sdk-model only when the operation needs them, and place the consumer method on the relevant service in sdk-api. Specify validation, required context, capability behavior, cancellation, and failure results before wiring UI.
  2. Implement shared rules in the corresponding internal runtime service. If the operation needs backend work, extend its narrow provider port and both adapters. If it is SDK-local library/history/progress work, use the existing store boundary; do not invent a matching backend provider solely for naming symmetry.
  3. Keep work tied to the captured authorization and shared session. A result begun for an old activation must not publish as current data after an account/profile switch. Use the existing session guards instead of duplicating lifecycle state in the new service.
  4. Connect application actions, state, and effects through the public service. Add a direct SDK contract case for failure and context behavior, plus a focused application test when observable navigation or rendering changes.

A progress-policy change belongs in RuntimePlaybackService and its recorder. Preserve the recorder's captured request/authorization, mutex, and cadence bookkeeping. The library already observes the actual playback service with matching authorization; introducing a second progress-only service or callback chain would create another route to reason about. Tests should exercise the real service design.

Add a provider with honest capabilities

Use the existing provider root factory/configuration pattern, canonical SDK package, and responsibility-based folders. Implement AuthProvider plus the account-bound ports assembled by ProviderSessionFactory. Supply backend content policy explicitly. Keep DTOs, transport credentials, and vendor exceptions internal; translate into shared values/errors at the adapter boundary. Advertise only implemented capabilities and return the agreed unsupported behavior for the rest. Authentication persistence is provider-owned; library, history, and progress remain SDK-local.

Register a new publication deliberately in StreamCoreSdkPublishingPlugin.kt and the verification tool's module/artifact inventories. Add supported platform factories and compile their actual targets; common source alone is insufficient. Add an independent coordinate consumer and shared-contract fixture. Provider-specific artwork or wording can live in a separate optional UI artifact if the application needs it. This is a template for future work, not a claim that a third provider already exists.

Change storage without changing the owner

Inspect the relevant preference repository, AccountStorageKey.kt, and PreferencesSdkStorage.kt together. Keys frame backend, namespace, account, and profile rather than concatenating ambiguous identifiers. The session supplies the authenticated owner; an expected-account restriction is not an identity source. Report malformed current-store data instead of silently resetting it. Verify restart, account separation, profile deletion, storage availability, and cancellation where the changed path can affect them.

Choose checks from the actual change. A mapper edit usually needs its mapper tests and relevant compilation. A shared runtime policy needs runtime and provider contracts. A public signature or dependency change also needs the staged coordinate consumer. Storage needs the affected platform restart checks. Add app UI/focus review for app behavior changes. Source-only maintenance does not require device bootstrap or an authenticated production build.

Exercise: propose a profile-scoped “hide title” operation

Write a short decision before code: is hiding a local library preference or a backend-synchronized operation? Define account/profile isolation, whether hidden titles disappear from home/search/saved lists, what happens on profile deletion, and whether both providers support it. Then name the service, runtime owner, optional provider work, store work, and smallest checks. There is no implemented hide-title feature here; the exercise tests whether the ownership decision precedes an abstraction.

quiz.question: A new saved-progress rule must apply identically to every provider. Where should it live?
options: In each platform PlayerViewModel so it can read playback UI state.
In each provider mapper so it is close to backend data.
In RuntimePlaybackService, verified through SDK behavior and the affected consumers.
quiz.explanation: Shared progress rules are SDK-owned. ViewModels report playback events and providers resolve media; duplicating policy there weakens provider and platform consistency.
